cells.tense: You're asking the questions you actually want answered, and the pull toward them is steady — it moves you without shoving.
cells.ask: Say the next question you're carrying out loud to one person before you've shaped the answer yourself, and watch their face while they take it in — a minute or less, information either way
cells.core:
You ask the real question now. Not the one that flatters you, not the one that gets agreement fastest — the one you actually want the answer to. The pull toward it is steady; it moves you without pushing.

When this part runs well you follow the question where it goes and take the next step without auditing the step to death. When it runs heavy the pull turns into ought: you pick up the question you're supposed to be asking and carry it like a job. Saying one live question to one person, before you've got the answer ready, shows you which of the two you're holding. Whatever their face tells you, it's yours to keep.
cells.sheetLine: You ask the real question now, and you know it's real.
cells.verb: learning what's true by asking into it and staying with the answer

cells.tense: You're already living past the moment — planning how the understanding will look once it's finished — while the learning that would make it true hasn't happened yet.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're learning your way through and stop explaining it for a day — just learn it, don't narrate it — then notice whether the pull got quieter or louder without the story
cells.core:
You're watching yourself learn. The finished version, the moment it lands — you're sketching it before it's true, and the sketch is doing the work the learning should be doing.

When this part is steady you study because studying is good, and the shine shows up on its own once something is actually finished. When it's running ahead, every hour at the desk is really about a future hour when someone notices. Trying harder here just feeds the same loop. Try less packaging instead: one topic, learned for a day without being made into a story, and the quiet you find will tell you where the pull was pointing.

cells.tense: You're still standing at a door you already went through — or one you decided not to — and calling it undecided while the present waits.
cells.ask: Ask one person what they want, something you don't already have the answer to, and stay quiet in their answer for a full minute before you say anything back — the asking and the quiet are one act
cells.core:
Something is known and it isn't being said out loud. Maybe a want is sitting there and you're calling it still open, or the pull has gone quiet and you're waiting for confirmation before you move. Either way, the direction isn't missing. The moving stopped.

When this is charged you decide by walking and the walking is how you find out. When it's drained, everything on the shelf looks like it could be the right thing, and the shelf is where you stay. Ask a person you're with what they actually want, hold their answer without correcting it, and you'll find your own pull in the shape of what you can care about in theirs.
cells.sheetLine: The direction is still there. You've stopped walking toward it.

cells.tense: You're already moving toward what draws you — you're just describing the movement as something that happened to you rather than something you're doing.
cells.ask: Say one thing you want out loud today, in plain words, to whoever's there — no case, no justification — and let the sentence stand after you've said it, without explaining what it meant
cells.core:
What's drawing you is already steering you. You notice yourself moving away from some things and toward others, and you explain it as circumstance or as being sensible. You're not lost. You just won't sign your name to the direction.

When this part is honest you want what you want and you say so, and other people can work with you because the direction is out in the open. When it's disowned, the pull keeps running and you keep calling it the situation. One sentence, spoken, with no argument attached, is what the living looks like from here: a plain want, named as a want. The fairness owed here starts with giving your own wanting a fair hearing.

attempts.check: The Enneagram-family vocabulary — Idealist/Catalyst/Investigator — is my inference from kernel archetype names, not stated in the record; if pressed I'd drop those words and describe the mechanism plainly. A reader might say the card is about wanting to learn, not about steering by a star, and they'd be half right: the card doesn't say they're lost, only that the star is unread. The ask at Too Much to picture the end does survive being wrong — noticing what's pictured can't misdirect; the Too Little ask to hear someone else's want is one action at a table, doable today, and survives. The only sentence that flatters the writer is the opening to Balanced — 'you're being pulled by something that's actually yours' — I kept it because it names the seat, not the person, and I stand behind it.

attempts.check: The rejected words were the card borrowing the seat's vocabulary back: I wrote 'star' because the record says star, but a stranger at a kitchen table has no star, and the machine is right that it reads as a product name. Same with 'the knowing' and 'the wanting' — I turned the person's own verbs into monuments. The unsupported move left in this draft is the Too Much line about rehearsing the reveal; the record says only that the capacity runs ahead of its timing, not that there's an audience, so I've cut the shine and kept the running-ahead. A reader could fairly say the questions don't need an audience either, and the balance cell survives that: offering one sentence to someone is an act, not an emotion, and if the read is wrong it still taught them something about what they actually think. The sentence that served the writer more than the reader was the Too Much sheet line about glowing — it admired its own image; it's gone.

attempts.check: The remaining refusals were mostly small echoes: 'What comes back is' and 'The way back isn't' are house phrasings I keep reaching for, and 'weather' was a borrowed image from a prior cell of mine. The Too Much cell still had 'knowing' as a noun, which I've turned back into a verb. In the Unacknowledged ask I had slipped into first person — 'here is one thing I want' — which reads as the Reader, not the person, and belongs in live delivery, not on glass. What a reader could fairly push back on: the record says the pull is recognized rather than given; nothing says the person avoids saying what they want. That's my inference from the seat's fruition stage plus wisdom's balanced face, and it's the weakest link in the fourth cell — but I've phrased it as a location ('you won't sign your name to the direction') rather than a story about them, so if it's wrong they can say so and still use the act. The Too Much ask survives being wrong: taking a day off from narrating what they're learning teaches them something about their own pull whether or not the seat is right. The sentence serving the writer more than the reader was the Too Much sheet line about performing understanding — it was the writer's flourish. I've kept a version but dropped the flourish.
